utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before the witness takes the solemn declaration, we considered last night whether the few additional questions in chief for the last witness justified his coming here at half past 9.00 and being here perhaps for five or ten minutes, and we thought that that wasn't sensible in all the circumstances, and so there would just be a couple of outstanding questions, as I indicated, there might be for him upon his return. There is one witness for today, Major Rule, and he will be taken by Mr. Lopez-Terres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lopez-Terres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Are you Mr. Alistair Rule, born on the 20th of August, 1958?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You are now a major in the British Armed Forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: How long have you been in the British army?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: About 22 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Major Rule, you arrived in Bosnia in mid-October 1992. At that time, you were an officer at the 1st Cheshire Regiment, which was under the command of Lieutenant-Colonel Robert Stewart?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Did you leave Bosnia on the 16th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Before you were stationed with the unit under your command, that is, Company B in the regiment in Gornji Vakuf, did you stay for a few days in Nova Bila, which was close to Vitez, where the headquarters of your regiment were set up; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Major Rule, I'm going to show you a map of Central Bosnia on which I'm going to ask you to indicate the various villages that you're going to speak about during your testimony. The map is Z2612-7. You can see the map close up that way. Major Rule, in your testimony, you're going to mention various villages. You're going to speak specifically about the town of Split in Croatia. Could you show us on the map where that city is?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: It's not actually on the map here. Split itself is -- I suppose if I move it this way. Here. Here is Split (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: It's on the shore, that's right. You're also going to mention the cities of Gornji Vakuf --

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The city of Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: (Indicating)

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Prozor?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: (Indicating)

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You're going to speak about the Makljen Pass?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: (Indicating)

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Lastly, you're going to speak about Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: (Indicating)

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Vitez, Jajce?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: (Indicating)

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Lastly, Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you say what area was under your responsibility at the time that you carried out those duties within the Cheshire Regiment?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: My company's responsibility went from Bugojno in the north down as far as Jablanica in the south, including Prozor and Gornji Vakuf, so this area here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you. We're going to leave the map aside for a little while. Before you set up in Gornji Vakuf, did you go to Vitez with a unit of your regiment, and during that trip you noted that there were conflict areas between the Muslims and the Croats? Could you speak to us for a few moments about what you saw during that trip?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes. Before the whole of the battalion arrived in Bosnia, about four weeks beforehand, there was a reconnaissance party of the key officers in the battalion which was led by Colonel Stewart, the commanding officer. A group of about 15 officers and about five or six Land Rovers drove into Bosnia, up to Vitez, to have a look at what tasks were required and where the various locations -- where the various companies would be located in that area. I was given the task of setting up my company base in Gornji Vakuf, and as the reconnaissance party travelled into Central Bosnia, I was detached to Gornji Vakuf to have a look at the town and try and find a location for my company. Whilst I stayed in Gornji Vakuf, the remainder of the reconnaissance party went on up to Vitez to carry out their task up there. We found what we thought was a suitable location in Gornji Vakuf, and we stayed overnight in that location. We then drove up to Vitez the following day to meet up with the main group of the reconnaissance party. On the road between Gornji Vakuf and Novi Travnik, a small -- at the time, a small and narrow track with a number of villages along the road, we realised that tensions were very high and there were lots of roadblocks preventing our way up to Vitez. We had to negotiate our way through each of the roadblocks until we came to a small village called Bugojcici just before we got to Novi Travnik, and we were unable to pass through this roadblock. There was an incident where there was a short gun battle which we were involved in, but we were told that Novi Travnik -- and we could clearly hear fighting in Novi Travnik, and we were told that it was unsafe for us to pass through.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Who held the roadblock? Who was manning it?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: The town of Bugojcici was a Muslim town, and it was armed by local inhabitants, local people from Bugojcici, and they were Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Did you notice whether the inhabitants of Bugojcici were wearing uniforms? Did they look like regular soldiers? Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: They didn't look like regular soldiers. They were armed. They were wearing a variety of combat clothing, but they didn't look like a formed unit of an army. They appeared to me to be local people who had armed themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: What kind of weapons did they have?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: They were carrying automatic weapons, light automatic weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: When you were blocked at the roadblock in Bugojcici, what happened? Do you remember what happened then?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: It was a truck, in fact, bore down on the roadblock, and there was a short gun battle. I didn't see any casualties. But immediately after that incident, I was able to quickly pass through the roadblock and travel on up to Vitez, and that was really our first knowledge that there was trouble there at all. I mean this came as a complete surprise to us, as we expected to have a fairly easy trip into Vitez to be able to carry out our task.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: When you arrived in Vitez with the members of your detachment, did you note or notice that the situation in that city or that area was also very tense, that is, in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Initially, we didn't notice anything particularly untoward in the Vitez area. We travelled -- that afternoon, after I had travelled up to Vitez, we went up to Nova Bila, which was just outside of Vitez. We travelled into the town itself of Vitez to meet up with the UNHCR representative, I believe he was Anders Levinsen, to discuss UNHCR issues. Although we believed it to be slightly tense, it seemed to be quite normal there because there were children running around the street and coming up to the vehicles and saying hello to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Did you notice whether there were any armed HVO soldiers in the city?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: We saw a number of armed soldiers in and around the town of Vitez, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: When you went to what was going to be your regiment's headquarters in Nova Bila, did you notice there was a roadblock that had been set up nearby? Could you speak to us about that roadblock?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: I can't hear properly through these -- it doesn't seem to be loud enough. I can't hear the translation. Could somebody speak --

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Is that better now? Can you hear?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: No, please speak louder. Again?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Do you hear better now?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: That's much better, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: When you went back to what was going to be your headquarters in Nova Bila -- that is, your regiment -- did you notice that a roadblock had been set up nearby, and could you speak to us about the roadblock?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: On the first day we went into Vitez, we travelled -- after we had spoken with the UNHCR, we travelled back to the school in Nova Bila where the battalion was based, and then we returned that night to Vitez to have some food. We noticed more roadblocks that evening, but no fighting as such. But again, we felt that the situation was becoming more tense. The following day, we went back into Vitez to -- well, Colonel Stewart led the recce, reconnaissance party, back into Vitez to try and meet up with the local commanders in Vitez. During that time, we realised that something was very wrong. There were roadblocks all the way into Vitez, and we could hear sporadic bursts of gunfire. Whilst we were in the town of Vitez, and Colonel Stewart was speaking with one of the local commanders, there were a number of bursts of fire which caused us to take cover ourselves and to make ready our own weapons. Colonel Stewart continued to speak to some commanders and was basically led to the impression that the problems were centred on the town of Novi Travnik, and so at about lunchtime, we travelled back to Vitez -- sorry, to the school in Nova Bila. On the way back, we came to a number of checkpoints which were difficult to get through.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In respect of those roadblocks, were there both HVO fighters and Muslim fighters?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes, on separate roadblocks. Depending on, obviously, the areas, one would be an HVO roadblock; the next one might be a Muslim checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You said a few minutes ago that when you went to Vitez for the first time, that you saw soldiers who were walking about on the streets, and I was asking you whether these were HVO soldiers or not. Could you indicate whether you saw any insignia, HVO insignia on those uniforms that the soldiers were wearing?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: When we were in the centre of the town of Vitez, in the actual town itself, the soldiers were HVO, and indeed, that evening, when we went into a restaurant to eat, the soldiers that came into the restaurant and that were in the vicinity of the restaurant were also HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The roadblock that was set up near your camp in Nova Bila, you said that that was manned by people who were wearing clothes that were a little bit strange for that region. Could you tell us about that, please?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: There was a considerable checkpoint in Nova Bila itself just before you turn off on to a dirt track which took you up to the school where the base was. There was a large bus parked across the road with a number of anti-tank mines. There was quite a lot of sporadic shooting going on as we tried to negotiate our way through that checkpoint, and as soon as we arrived there, there didn't appear to be anybody manning it, because, obviously, of the danger of small-arms fire. So we had to try and find somebody to come and move the bus so that we could continue on our way. Eventually we did find somebody who we had to remonstrate with quite firmly to let us go through, and he was wearing the Eastern garb that you would expect a Mujahedin fighter to be wearing. He was wearing -- and he looked of a sort of Middle Eastern origin.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Was the roadblock manned exclusively by people who come from the near East? Were there other local soldiers who were Muslims as well?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: We saw only two or perhaps three people actually on that roadblock, and they were only Mujahedin, or wore the garb or the clothes that the Mujahedin would wear. Eventually, he jumped into the driver's seat of the coach, drove it away, moved the anti-tank mines, and we were allowed to pass through and then on up to the school. As we passed through, more fire came from that vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The facts that you're speaking about refer to the visit to Vitez, the roadblocks that you've mentioned. Was this all around the 20th of October, 1992? Is that the right time period?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes, round about then. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You said a few minutes ago that the main problem in that region was the one that was centred in Novi Travnik. Could you speak to us a little bit about the incidents that occurred in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: From the discussions that Colonel Stewart and I -- on not all occasions, but on some of the occasions I was with him, we were led to believe by those people in Vitez that the main fighting was in the town of Novi Travnik. Because all this fighting was preventing us from carrying out our main, our principal task, which was to reconnoitre the area so that we could prepare the way for the arrival of the main British force, we felt it necessary to try and calm the situation so that we could get on with our principal task, and Colonel Stewart made the decision to visit Novi Travnik that afternoon to try and find out what was going on there, to try and broker some kind of ceasefire. I didn't travel with him with that small party, but I know he went there, and I know that he witnessed quite a lot of fighting in the town of Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Did Colonel Stewart mention anything that he had seen in Novi Travnik, specifically the result of the brokering that he was able to conduct?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: He was not successful in brokering a ceasefire at that stage, and so he returned back to the camp at Nova Bila, just north of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: After that short stay there, you were commander of various liaison officers of your regiment, which meant that you would move about in the region between Gornji Vakuf, Split, and Nova Bila; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Correct. After we had had our not particularly successful reconnaissance, the main group of officers from the regiment returned to Split, where they went back to Germany to meet up with the regiment that was in Germany and preparing to deploy into Bosnia. We left behind a number of liaison officers in the area, particularly based in Vitez, and I, as the senior officer left behind with the regiment, was made responsible for the liaison officers. I therefore had a coordination role between the regimental liaison officers, who were based in Vitez, and also our British headquarters, which was based in Split. So I travelled between Gornji Vakuf, Split, and reconnoitred a number of different routes during that period to see what was available to us to use, what routes were available to us to use. And so I went through Mostar, I saw Prozor, I went to Jablanica, and obviously the road that we used from Gornji Vakuf, Vitez, and Prozor, back into Tomislavgrad and then into Croatia itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: During that period -- that is, around the end of October, 1992 -- you were informed by one of your liaison officers, Captain Hughes, that there had been fighting in Prozor -- Captain Hughes, that is; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: It was Captain Hughes. Captain Hughes was my own company liaison officer, and he also had a role to stay in touch with this isolated group of British officers who were based in the school, and he also had his own task of trying to discover what was going on, particularly in my own company's area in Gornji Vakuf. On one particular journey, he was travelling from Gornji Vakuf back down to Split and drove through or attempted to drive through the town of Prozor. He was unable to get through. He was prevented from getting through by, I believe, a roadblock. But also, he could see that there was quite a lot of fighting going on there. He could hear the fighting, and so he chose to try and find another route around to the north of Prozor and eventually discovered a track which could bypass the town. Whilst he was driving along this track, he was actually engaged by mortar fire and small-arms fire, and he managed to successfully get around this route and then bypass Prozor and then travel down to Split, where he reported the incident to me. He was obviously in quite an excited state, because he had been in quite a lot of danger as he had driven around Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Was he able to say what the source of the mortar fire was?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: No, he wouldn't have been able to locate where that fire was coming from.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Did you, yourself, have the chance to go to Prozor at the time that we're speaking about, and could you tell us what you saw when you were able to get into the city of Prozor?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Well, clearly, it was in our interests to be able to have free passage through Prozor, and so the fact that Prozor was closed off affected our potential plans for deploying into Central Bosnia because our major route passed through Prozor. So it was important that I went to try and find out what was happening in Prozor. I did pass through Prozor -- perhaps a day or two days later; I can't exactly remember -- and found damaged property, evidence of fighting, and -- yes, I mean, I went to Prozor a few days after the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And about the destruction of property which you saw, did you also see that perhaps some things were destroyed more than others?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: I mean, it was very clear that the whole of the town hadn't been destroyed at all. It was, in fact, in a pretty good state. What I did see, and was very marked, was that properties had been selectively destroyed. You know, you would get a group of three buildings which were perfectly intact and then a fourth building which was burnt out. And that's what I saw. That was the destruction that I saw in the town of Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In your statement, you told about signs of ethnic cleansing in Prozor. Could you perhaps elaborate on that point?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I object to any reference to the witness statement, Your Honour. Obviously, that's not in evidence. The witness is here to give his own testimony. I also object to the leading nature of that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, perhaps you could rephrase that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You have just told us about selective destruction of the town. Did you also see any particular signs which might make you think that Muslim property was particularly targeted?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: When I passed through the town of Prozor, it was -- I was not able to -- I am not able to say that the properties which I saw that had been destroyed were specifically Muslim properties. However, obviously as head of the liaison officers, it was my task to speak to people in the local community, and the general impression that I gained from the Muslims that I had spoken to was that their properties had been targeted in Prozor and it was, in fact, the Muslim population that had been driven out of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: On that occasion, you met Anders Levinsen, whom you just mentioned, whom you had already met in Vitez. Could you share with us the conversation that you had with Mr. Levinsen?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: During that three- to four-week period, I had quite a lot of dealings with Mr. Levinsen, and obviously it was my job to make sure that we had a good working relationship with the UNHCR. On a discussion I had shortly after travelling through Prozor, he stated to me that families, Muslim families, had been driven out into the hills south of Prozor as a result of the fighting that had gone on, the recent fighting that had gone on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: When you entered the town of Prozor, did you have the feeling that the town was in the hands of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: I know that the town was completely in the hands of the HVO and the police. I went to the HVO headquarters and spoke to the local commander to try and find out from his side what had happened, and there were absolutely no BiH soldiers at all in the town and the town was completely controlled by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: At the time that we are talking about, the town of Jajce also fell; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes. Although I had responsibility for all the liaison officers of the battalion, I was also very interested in my own company's area of responsibility, which was Gornji Vakuf, and I met all the local commanders and spoke to all the important people in the town. During that period, the town of Jajce fell, and this was a significant -- it appeared to be significant to me, because I could see a real dip in the morale of the Muslim people in Jajce. Jajce wasn't expected. They didn't -- at the time, they didn't expect Jajce to fall, and when it did do, they were very, very depressed when they heard the news that Jajce had fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: As we are talking about the fall of Jajce, we are evidently talking about its falling into the Serb hands?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes. The Serbs captured the town of Jajce, and the belief within the Muslim community was that a previously-strong position had been made untenable because of the withdrawal of the HVO soldiers in the Jajce area, and that was their belief and that is why they felt the town of Jajce had fallen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you very much for these things that you told us, and now let us move to the period of time when you were on duty in Gornji Vakuf. As you told us at the beginning, you were posted to Gornji Vakuf in November 1992 until the 16th of January, 1993, is that so, and you also told us that your company, B Company, was quartered in that town and that it was in an old factory which was originally used by the Bosnian army; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: That's correct. In fact, it wasn't an old factory, it was a very new factory, and it was ideal for our purposes. It had all the services. Electricity and power were very modern and very good, and it was just the location I needed. So we entered into negotiation with the BiH, who were controlling the factory at that time, as to whether or not we could use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I will now show you a map of the Gornji Vakuf area, and here we have the 17th of January, 1993, and we have here the HVO positions and Bosnian army positions. It was a map which we used at the time. Could you please show us, where was your company in the town of Gornji Vakuf? It is Z227A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, have we got this map?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) It is at the end of the list of documents that was handed over to you this morning. You do not have it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, we have got it. It's 2761.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Will you please show us, where is the place that your company used at the time?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: It is actually ringed there (indicating). It's a little bit unclear because it's a photocopied map, but this was the factory which we used here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Please show us where the HVO headquarters was.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: This appeared to be some sort of light industrial area of the town (indicating), and immediately adjacent to my barracks was the HVO headquarters, which was just here (indicating), and there was an area of land around my location, a small, relatively insubstantial fence, which then led directly onto the HVO headquarters and the factory that they were using. Just to give you an idea, the centre of town is on this crossroads here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: How far were you from the centre of Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Well, as the crow flies, from right in the centre, we were no more than 800 metres from the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you. As for this factory that you used, you told us that in the beginning, that there was a dispute in the beginning about the payment, wasn't there; about the rent, actually?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes, and which did continue sporadically. Obviously, I was extremely keen to secure this factory as a base for my company for the reasons I've told you, and I entered directly into negotiation with the people that were occupying the building at that time, who were the BiH. And as such, we dealt directly with them and the agreement we came to was directly with them, and we agreed to pay them 10.000 Deutschmarks a month for the use of the factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The local HVO, did they also ask for a share of this rent?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: One of the problems that I had in the early stages of my tour in Gornji Vakuf was to try and reconcile the problems that the HVO had raised, because they believed that they should have a share of the money that we were paying to the BiH. To my knowledge, that was never resolved, and we continued to pay the 10.000 marks to the BiH and not to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: At the time we are talking about, you mostly focused on reconciling the parties and bringing closer together local commanders, the HVO commander and the Bosnian army commander, and you conducted numerous negotiations with them, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: It was always an implied task set upon me, as the company commander in Gornji Vakuf, to certainly try and create an atmosphere within my area of responsibility which allowed for the easy transit of humanitarian aid through the area and to those areas that needed it, and, you know, that was more than just putting a vehicle in front and at the rear of a convoy. It was maintaining an atmosphere within the area where vehicles could transit freely. Because of that, and clearly allowed to by my commander, I was involved in a lot of discussion, almost daily discussion, with the various commanders in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You also met the commander of the HVO, Mr. Tokic, and the commander of the Bosnian army, and his name was Agic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes. I got to know both Agic and Tokic extremely well, and I would say that I had a good working and friendly relationship with both men.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Those two men, did they know one another before the conflict broke out in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: I believe that they had known each other before, before the conflict in Bosnia, and had previously served in the JNA together.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Your conciliatory mission between the local protagonists, was it successful and were you able to set up your information teams which were able to collect as much reconnaissance information as possible in the area? Could you please tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: As I was fortunate -- well, I had the -- I was the company with its own territorial area of responsibility. Therefore, I was responsible for knowing what was going on in the area in which I operated. And it is certainly a well tried and tested system within the British army which sets up or which has set up, in operations in other parts of the world, procedures for gathering low-level information. My own battalion and my own senior non-commissioned officers and junior non-commissioned officers would have had experience in Northern Ireland in looking for -- looking, as they were out in the area, looking for interesting occurrences, looking for unusual things that were happening, and we set up our own military information cell which was headed up by a colour-sergeant who was in my company. It was very much one of our first priorities, to find out exactly what was happening in the area, and because of this all patrols, and this is a standard procedure within the British army, particularly at company level where you are responsible for an area, it is a well-known and well-practised procedure to set up such a military information cell. So each individual soldier, for example, would be issued with an aide-memoire of equipment so that he could pick out equipment that he spotted perhaps when he was out on a patrol and report it back. Every patrol, before it went out, would have been briefed by my military information sergeant. He would give them tasks to look out for certain things, and at the end of a patrol, when they came back in again, the whole patrol would be sat down and he personally would then debrief them to get out all the sightings that they had seen, any interesting equipment, any interesting shoulder badges, any interesting insignia which they had spotted. So we had these permanent eyes and ears, as it were, using my soldiers and also using my liaison officer and myself, who conducted liaison with the local commanders and picking up information from them. So that would be brought together and then sent off daily in the form of an information -- a military information summary to my battalion headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: So summaries of military information were known commonly as infosums; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: That is the abbreviated form, infosum, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: How many men did you have, more or less, under your commander in order to gather all this information?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Well, under my immediate command, I had about 140 soldiers, and obviously they formed the -- when they were tasked to carry out, you know, a particular patrol, they would form the basis of all the military information that I gained. But also a lot of administrative traffic were passed through us; you know, resupply from Split. They drove up through Prozor, sometimes they drove up through Mostar and Jablanica, and if they had seen anything interesting, they would have reported it to me as well. So whenever a British soldier was out on the ground driving a vehicle, conducting a patrol, he would be automatically looking around him, looking for interesting pieces of equipment, you know, any unusual things that were going on, and it's almost, you know, inbred into them to be inquisitive like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The system of information gathering was applied throughout the area of responsibility, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: So there were daily reports which were drawn up in every municipality under your jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes. I produced -- (French interpretation)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're getting French. Let's see if we can get on.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes. I would have been responsible for gathering information from my area of responsibility, and the other companies, wherever they were operating, would have also been responsible for providing a milinfosum to battalion headquarters, who would put it together and pass it then on further up the chain of command. MR.LOPEZ-TERRES: (Interpretation) I should like the usher to show you a map which we used in the beginning, Z2612. This is a coloured map.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you show us the town of Gornji Vakuf on this map?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: (Indicating)

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The location at which this town was situated was of strategic value, was of strategic importance, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes, certainly we believed it to be. As you can see, it sits on two routes, one coming from the Travnik-Vitez area and one passing up to Bugojno. This route itself, at the time, was really the only route which people could pass up and our own administrative transport could pass up, because this road here between Bugojno and Novi Travnik, the Serb front lines were up here somewhere, and so it was always very dangerous passing along this route. So all administrative traffic would go up here (indicating), and this route was constantly under threat, and I myself would only go up that route in armoured vehicles. So if you sit on this area here, then it's of key importance. It was certainly of key importance to us, as a battalion, as well to ensure that we could keep these routes into the main battalion area, up here, open.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you. And the Gornji Vakuf population was mostly Muslim, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: The majority was Muslim, yes, but there was a significant Croat, but also a small Serb population as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: During your stay there, you noted a number of incidents in the municipality of Gornji Vakuf, and in particular, you reported an incident which happened in November 1992, an incident in which an HVO soldier beheaded a man?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes. This was the first real major problem that I had as a company commander in Gornji Vakuf. The Muslim authorities and the Muslim commander came to me the day -- the morning after the event, telling me about this incident that had happened the night before. Apparently -- none of my soldiers witnessed it, but apparently the night before, a Croatian soldier who had been on the front line near to Gornji Vakuf, above Gornji Vakuf, on the mountain of Radusa, had come back, was drunk, and had cut off the head of a Muslim, a paraplegic, someone who was in a wheelchair, and tossed his head into a Muslim-owned bar. Now, whilst none of my soldiers witnessed it, the HVO commander also came to my headquarters, and they admitted that yes, this had happened, and that the soldier in question had been removed to Mostar for investigation. The problem was that the Muslims wanted to take the soldier to Zenica to try him there and to deal with him in Zenica, whilst the soldier himself was in Mostar, and the HVO were stating that he would be dealt with in Mostar. The Muslims didn't feel that he would be dealt with properly in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: A while ago, you mentioned the reports which were drawn up in Gornji Vakuf, the milinfosums, and I will now show you the report of the 18th of November, 1992. Could you tell us if this report covers this incident that you spoke about? It is Z2981. Will you please look at pages 2 and 3 of the report.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Right. This is the milinfosum from the battalion headquarters, so it's not the milinfosum that would have come from Gornji Vakuf to Vitez. It was the one after all the information had been correlated and then passed on to the superior headquarters. This section here is dealing with Gornji Vakuf and Bugojno, and there is an extract of a conversation I had had with the commander in Bugojno, and his -- his concerns with Serbs -- with the Serb objectives in and around Bugojno. But it also deals with the occurrence in Gornji Vakuf, here: "In Gornji Vakuf, tensions are reported to be high due to the HVO taking over a building belonging to the Bosnian army. This was escalated when" -- this individual here, Rajic -- "beheaded a local Muslim with a sheet of glass while drunk and possibly on drugs. The victim was reported to be a paraplegic. The Muslims wanted Vlatko to go on trial in Zenica while the HVO said they would put him on trial in Mostar. The Muslims are now reported to have taken 10 Croats prisoner, and tensions are still running high." So that accurately reflects what happened, and it was written -- you know, either on that day or the following day of that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The report mentions, the report you've just read out, on the last part of page 2, that a building was taken by the HVO, a building which belonged to the BH army. Could you speak to us about that, give us some clarification about the taking of that building?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't. My memory is -- I don't recall that particular incident, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The soldier who was taken to Mostar, according to what was said to you by representatives of the HVO, do you know whether he was prosecuted criminally for having killed that Muslim?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: I don't know, and the -- you know, over time, the tensions that were raised as a result of that particular incident did calm down. However, I did hear it later reported to me from the Muslim side that this --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't mean to interrupt Mr. Lopez-Terres's presentation, but I think that the witness is actually reciting hearsay, not from something that he heard, but several times removed, from unidentified sources, who themselves may have heard it from other sources. So I think that that sort of unreliable evidence really doesn't have any use before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, that's a matter for us to say. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes. Remembering that I did have daily discussions with commanders, and it was my -- you know, it was my job to find out exactly what was happening in the local region, then it was reported to me that this soldier had been seen back on the front line, apparently free.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Lopez-Terres, to bring us closer to the facts in this testimony, could we ask Major Rule what the exact terms of his mission on the ground were? What instructions did he, himself, have in respect of what he had to do in the field? He would give out certain information, but he received instructions, conduct that he had to maintain. Could we have some ideas about that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation).

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Would you answer that question, Major Rule, about the specific nature of the mission assigned to you?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Well, the specific nature of the mission assigned to me was to aid the delivery of humanitarian aid to -- through my area and to those locations in my area that needed it. And clearly it was therefore an implied task set upon me that if I could possibly do it, I would have to create, if it was within my power, to create an environment in which humanitarian aid could pass freely through my area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, but, Major Rule, did you have a function which was to maintain order? Or to try to carry out your humanitarian work, did you use force yourself in order to ensure that the humanitarian mission could be conducted properly?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: We never used force at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Could you use your weapons in self-defence?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: We would only use our weapons in self-defence. In no other scenario.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I would like us to go back to the incident of the 18th of November and the death of the Muslim who had been killed by the HVO soldier. You had just told us that after the information that you had at that time, the soldier was seen again in the field in the Gornji Vakuf region, that is, some time after the crime was committed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And did you receive that information before you left Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: I was aware of that information before I left Gornji Vakuf, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: So that was around the 18th of November, and the information was prior to your departure in January of 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes. And I believe it to be fairly -- it was shortly before I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: So this is now the end of 1992. While you were in Gornji Vakuf, did you have the feeling that the HVO was putting increasing pressure on the Muslim population of the city?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: It was reported to me on numerous occasions that the checkpoint on Makljen -- I don't know if you wish me to point that out -- there was a high pass to the south of Gornji Vakuf which was the only route from Prozor into Gornji Vakuf. This was held by the HVO from Prozor, and they frequently would close the road off, not allow Muslims to pass through, would attempt to charge them tolls for passing through, through the checkpoint. And also, on numerous occasions, I dispatched myself and my own liaison officer to try and discover what was going on. But it was a frequent occurrence, on this particular checkpoint, where access was denied to Muslims. There were also numerous other sightings, sightings of soldiers, sightings of equipment which -- and my soldiers would have daily passed over this route -- reported back to me, which led me to believe that there was a certain amount of reinforcing that was going on in the Prozor area, and specifically in and around the Makljen area as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Did you also see, in the buildings or around the buildings of the HVO headquarters in Gornji Vakuf, did you see that there was construction, or that things were being reinforced?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes. There was a particular occasion where we saw, because the barracks was immediately adjacent to us, reinforcing, trenches being dug, more activity, more vehicular activity in and around the barracks. And that happened some time before Christmas. We also -- for example, my soldiers spotted what appeared to be a regular -- regular troops, with a Tiger badge on their soldiers, a Tiger badge which they would have had in their aide-memoires, so they would have realised the significance or otherwise of the individual badges. They were well equipped. They were also seeing, I think, up to about two platoons, I believe, were seen -- that's about 60 soldiers -- were seen in the Makljen area. And these soldiers stuck out particularly because they weren't like the irregular soldiers which they had become used to. They were well equipped, tidy, and wore a proper uniform as opposed to a mishmash of uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: After the information -- according to the information that you had at that time, did the Tiger Regiment soldiers that you've just spoken about, would you say that they were HVO soldiers or soldiers from a different army?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Our deduction from the sighting -- the fact was that the soldiers were seen with this badge, they were dressed in a certain manner, our deduction from that, our military information deduction from that, was that these were regular HV [LiveNote read in error "HVO"] soldiers from the Tiger Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I would like to be sure that the interpretation was correct. Here it says that they were regular soldiers, or professional soldiers, of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: HV.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: All right. So there is a mistake in the French transcript, and in this transcript, it says "HVO," but when you're speaking -- you're speaking about "HV," but when you say "HV," you mean the Croatian army soldiers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: (Inaudible)

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to review another milinfosum report. This is the one, 45, which is the 16th of December, 1992. This exhibit is Z298,2. Could you have a look at the second page of the document, please. Does this report suitably represent the facts that we're speaking about? Are you able to read it?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you wish me to read it? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: No, no, don't read it out loud. I just want to know whether this mentions the facts that you were speaking about.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You spoke about the Makljen pass that had been reinforced and about the fact that the soldiers wearing the Tiger Brigade (sic) were seen; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: That's correct. And that refers to this, here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: More or less at the same time -- thank you, Mr. Usher -- at the time that we're speaking about, that is, December of 1992, do you remember whether in Gornji Vakuf there were HOS soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: We had numerous sightings of HOS soldiers, both from my own soldiers and reported to me by the Muslim commanders. The HOS were quite easy to pick out because they were -- they always wore black, and in fact they wrote "HOS" on their vehicles, and so it was relatively easy to spot them when they were around. And yes, we had numerous sightings on them on the leadup to Christmas and after Christmas as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Around Christmas 1992, specifically around the 21st of December, do you remember that the HVO reinforced its positions near Prozor in the village which is known as Kovacevo Polje?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: No, it wasn't reinforced. My liaison officer -- I believe it was my liaison officer, but it was certainly one of my patrols -- reported military equipment, more military equipment and heavy equipment in the area of -- I think it's Kovacevo Polje. Yes, that was reported to me, and I dispatched my liaison officer to go and confirm whether or not that was, indeed, the case, which he did do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: He was able to see that, in fact?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Did your soldiers also see that there was vehicle movement, communications in the area?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yeah. Yes, again, the significance of certain items of equipment would have been well known to my soldiers. They would have been shown pictures of it. They would have had their own individual aide-memoires. And I know that in particular, a command vehicle was spotted, a six-wheeled command vehicle was spotted by one of my patrols at around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In respect of this communication system that the HVO had available to it, did you notice that they had a very effective, even sophisticated communication system?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: There are two specific incidents that lead me or showed me that actually the systems of communications available to the HVO were extremely effective. The first one was that on a visit to the HVO headquarters, I was asked -- we were discussing nonmilitary matters, and I mentioned my own wife and family back in Germany and how my soldiers were a bit frustrated because they had been in Gornji Vakuf for so long and were unable to speak to their families because we didn't have the communications available to us. He was very surprised when he heard this, and said, you know, "When was the last time you spoke to your wife?" I said, "About six weeks ago." He said, "Come in here," and he took me into a communications room which had various items of communication equipment. And I was able to pick up a phone, dial my wife in Germany, and speak to her for the first time in six weeks. So that was one. I had immediate communications outside of Gornji Vakuf, where we had been told that none such existed. Certainly the infrastructure didn't allow that. Obviously we had our own military systems of communications, which we were unable to use for our own personal use. So that was one thing that I personally witnessed. The second was much later on, after fighting had broken out in Gornji Vakuf. We -- I had both commanders in my headquarters who -- and we were attempting to arrange a ceasefire, and we in fact had tacitly agreed that a ceasefire would take place at a given time; I can't remember the exact time. The time passed with both these commanders in my headquarters. There was a flurry of mortar rounds, of small-arms fire, immediately after the deadline, and the HVO commander picked up a small hand-sized commercial-type radio -- a UHF, I believe, type radio -- and got on to the radio immediately, in a very angry manner, that people were not obeying his command, and ten other -- about ten other stations answered up immediately to his call. Now, that was certainly better communication than I had available to me using the VHF radios that I was operating, VHF and HF radios that I was operating. I certainly couldn't communicate in and around Gornji Vakuf that effectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Major Rule, in January 1993, there was an incident which had to do with the raising of a flag in Gornji Vakuf by the HVO. Could you speak about that, please?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes. The -- and I saw the flag myself; I remember quite clearly that right on the crossroads, on a lamppost at the crossroads, an Ustasha flag was raised in the -- or somebody put a Ustasha flag up in the centre of town, and I drove past it and realised straightaway that that was going to cause quite a lot of tension in the town. Later on it was reported to me that a Muslim soldier went up and took the flag down, and whilst he was doing that was actually shot at, whilst that was happening. And that was just one incident which generally and gradually increased the tension that we were perceiving was happening in the town. And I believe that shortly after that, Muslims put up their own checkpoints to control movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) If the usher would show the witness Z2983. The document is another milinfosum. This is number 67, dated the 6th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you have a look at this document, specifically paragraph 2 of page 1? Does this refer to the incident that you've just spoken about?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: No, that's another incident. In fact, that call sign was my own vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I'm speaking about paragraph 2, where it has to do with a Ustasha flag.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Sorry. Got it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Does this refer to the incident?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes. It just cut out for a second there. Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: So this was the 5th or 6th of January, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You have just told us that checkpoints were set up, -- thank you, Mr. Usher -- that is, checkpoints were set up in the city after that incident. Were there many of those checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: I can't be absolutely specific, but all I recall is that there were a number of checkpoints that -- of course, this is what always happened whenever there was a raising of tensions, and it was always indicative that tensions had been raised, when these roadblocks suddenly appeared, and that was certainly an indicator to us that things weren't -- that tensions were rising.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Do you remember a bomb or some kind of explosives in the hotel that was used by the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes. Leading up to the major breakout of fighting that I witnessed in Gornji Vakuf, the incident that seemed to spark it off, the final incident that seemed to spark it off, was a bomb which was planted in a hotel again on the crossroads in Gornji Vakuf, which was a Muslim-owned hotel and was some form of headquarters which they used. A bomb went off, I believe, in the early hours of the morning. I seem to remember that it was the early hours of the morning. It was after that that a general outbreak of fighting actually happened, after that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: During the night that you're speaking about, was there shelling of some of the city of Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Throughout the day, there was sporadic fighting which got more intense, and I remember, during the night, walking around my company position. It was quite a large area, fenced area, and I, with my sergeant major, were walking around the position, because I had lots of sentries out, obviously, because I was concerned for the security of my camp. And whilst I was walking around, we saw and witnessed heavy shells coming into the town, and we heard the detonations and the flashes of heavy-calibre artillery which was coming into the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Do you remember shelling that the Serbs did on the city?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: When that shelling occurred and from where I stood, it appeared that the shelling was coming from the north of the town because you could hear the sound of the shell coming in, and I assumed at that stage that -- or my deduction was at that stage that it was actually HVO shelling. But I discovered the next day, and it was the Muslims themselves that said this to me, that actually it wasn't HVO shelling at all, it was the Serbs shelling from the other side of the mountain and that it was actually they that had engaged the town of Gornji Vakuf with heavy artillery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, it's now 11.00. Is that a convenient moment to adjourn?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll take a break for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Major Rule, before this short break, you spoke about the shelling of the town of Gornji Vakuf, shelling by Serb forces. This shelling which you witnessed, was it the only one in the town of Gornji Vakuf at the time when you were there?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: At the time that -- I can't say whether or not that was the only shelling that I witnessed. That was the most -- because the town was quiet at the time, that the shelling seemed much more vivid, you know, and I could single it out very clearly. But in subsequent days, there was a lot of mortar fire, and it would be very difficult for me to differentiate between what was mortars and what was shelling in that particular situation. That night was a quiet, clear night, and it was very evident of what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: But it was therefore the only time -- according to information that you received at the time, it was the same time when it was alleged that the Serbs aimed their fire at the town during your stay there?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: During that period, that was the only time that it was reported to us that the Serbs were shelling -- had shelled the town, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Was any particular part of the town aimed at by those who carried out the shelling?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: It was very clearly evident to where I stood with my sergeant major that the shells were landing in generally the northern part of the town, the northwestern part of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Who lived in that part of the town? Which ethnic community was the majority there?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: I believe it to have been Muslim, a majority Muslim area of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: During that period of time around the 12th of January, 1993, you also took note of various troop movements, in particular again, around the area of Makljen and in the locality of Podgrade?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes. We continued -- throughout the conflict, we continued to conduct patrolling obviously in our armoured vehicles, and we continued to gather information, as far as we could, as to what was happening in the area. Certainly, it was reported to us that Podgrade, which was to the northwest of Gornji Vakuf, had been reinforced by HVO, and indeed the Makljen itself was reinforced also by HVO equipment and soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: According to you, was there any particular military reason to undertake those reinforcements?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Podgrade is immediately to the north, Makljen is immediately to the south. That seals off those two routes into the town, so one encircled Gornji Vakuf, and also one would presume that Bugojno -- there was a large concentration of Muslim forces in Bugojno, and that it would form some sort of barrier to prevent reinforcement of Gornji Vakuf from soldiers from Bugojno, Muslim soldiers from Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You already told us, and you told us now again, about various movements of HVO troops in the area under your responsibility. Troops, vehicles which were moving about, could you see or did your soldiers see that any of these vehicles were carrying ammunition, or anything like that, either in Gornji Vakuf or between Novi Travnik and Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: It would have been very difficult to discover the nature of the loads that were being carried on vehicles that were in enclosed -- you know, under canopies and in the bodies of a vehicle. So, yes, we would have spotted the vehicles, but we would have been unable to know what was actually inside the vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Major Rule, to your knowledge were there 120- or 148-millimetre mortars used by the HVO in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: There was a lot of mortar fire. Certainly, our deductions would have been that there were two principal mortars available to the HVO. One was a 120-millimetre mortar and one was an 82-millimetre mortar, and we believe both were used during the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I will now show you a document, Major, which is Z2481A. This document is dated 10th of January, 1993, and it is Major Luka Sekerija, who was one of the commanding officers of the Ante Starcevic Brigade in Gornji Vakuf. Would you look at this document? It is, in point of fact, a request for the supply -- for the procurement of shells requested by Major Luka Sekerija from his superior, Colonel Blaskic, and from the vice-president of Herceg-Bosna, Dario Kordic. At the time that we are talking about, that is, January 1993, if I understood you properly, it was quite easy for the HVO to secure the supply of ammunition from Vitez to Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yeah. That amount of shells wouldn't have been particularly difficult to transport. It wouldn't have required a lot of vehicles at all; one or two perhaps. So, yes, that would have been relatively easy for them to resupply their forces in Gornji Vakuf with that number of shells, mortar bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Do you know, did you meet Mr. Luka Sekerija during your posting there?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: I did know Luka, yes. Most of my discussions were with who I believed to be the commander, Zrinko Tokic, but I certainly met, on numerous occasions, Luka, who I believed to be a senior officer within his organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: After the conflict broke out around the 11th, 12th, or 13th of January, you explained that the local brigade commanders tried to arrive at a ceasefire between the two parties?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: On the second day of the fighting, I had a visit actually in my location by Zrinko Tokic, who I believed to be the commander of the HVO forces in Gornji Vakuf, and he told me that he had a direct field telephone link with the Muslim headquarters and that he had spoken to the Muslim commander, who had agreed that they needed to come and speak, and they obviously chose my location to speak because it was a neutral location. Although there was a lot of fighting going on in the town at the time, I agreed that I would provide my armoured vehicles to go down into the town and to speak with the Muslim commander and bring him back to my location in the factory so that we could discuss some sort of ceasefire. I did that. I went down myself with my vehicle and two other vehicles. We went into the Muslim headquarters. There was a certain amount of discussion. He wasn't absolutely convinced that he should come, but in the end I persuaded him to come with me, and we came back to my location, where they had discussions about how to negotiate a ceasefire.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: At that particular moment, the negotiations were being undertaken only by local commanders; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Only by Zrinko Tokic and Fahrudin Agic, who were in command of the opposing forces in Gornji Vakuf at that time. The negotiations were, indeed, friendly and constructive, and there seemed to be no antagonism between the two men.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: During the negotiations, it was decided to call upon other authorities outside the town, and it is how, I'm sure, that your superior was invited to join in the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: It became apparent during the negotiation that although both men were committed to restore peace in the town, that it was outside or it was beyond their command status. They needed to raise it in importance, and, in fact, they suggested that there should be a meeting the following day again at my headquarters of more senior officers from the HVO and from the BiH. When they suggested that to me, it was at that stage that I felt that it would be appropriate to also ask my commanding officer, Colonel Bob Stewart, to come down and also represent the U.N. at those talks, and it was agreed that that would take place at 10.00 the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: At the date of meeting, when was it that Colonel Edwards and his soldiers were killed?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes. That morning, Colonel Stewart, with a platoon from my company that had been attached to Colonel Stewart, drove down from Vitez to Gornji Vakuf and arrived early in the morning at my location. Shortly after he arrived, a civilian ambulance arrived at the front gate of my barracks. There was a driver, who stated that he had two casualties in the back of his ambulance, two civilian casualties, and he wished to be able to drive his ambulance through the town so that he could get these casualties to Prozor, because there was a functioning hospital in Prozor. I agreed to this request and allocated and instructed one of my platoons to escort that ambulance through the town. As they approached the centre of town, crossing a bridge over a river, one of the drivers of one of the vehicles was shot in the head and was killed, and that was Corporal Wayne Edwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And the negotiations began with Colonel Stewart; do you remember the names of persons representing the HVO in those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: I remember the names. The names that I remember clearly were Merdan from the Muslim side, from Zenica, and Andric from the HVO side, from Mostar. And the other name, it was Siljeg, as well, from the HVO side; and the other member of the Muslim side was, I believe, called Seljo. I remember him as Seljo. So it was Merdan and Seljo on the Muslim side and Andric and Siljeg on the HVO side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: So, according to you, who was the head, who was the one who conducted negotiations on behalf of the HVO that day?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: The person that was doing all the talking was Andric.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you recount in a few words, what did he say, what were his requests during those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: The negotiations went on for some time, and then eventually he read out a statement requiring the Muslims to lay down their arms, and I'm -- you know, I'm paraphrasing what I believe to -- what I remember -- to lay down the Muslim arms and basically accept that the HVO were going to assume control of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I understand, of course, that it was a long time ago and that you therefore have difficulty in remembering the exact words of Colonel Andric, but I will show you a document which is a milinfosum which is of the 16th January, 1993, and which is document Z298,5, the 16th of January, 1993, milinfosum. I should like to ask you to look at page 3, and it is a paragraph at the bottom of that page and on top of page 4, that is, the end of page 3 and beginning of page 4. Would you then look at the end of it on page 4. Does this report speak about the terms laid by Colonel Andric that you just spoke about?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes, that's absolutely it. And, at one stage, Andric used slightly more blunt language and actually stated that if the BiH didn't agree to the demands, he would flatten Gornji Vakuf. And I heard that myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: How did the Muslim party respond to those threats or those terms?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: The Muslim party were very concerned. They were -- you know, attempting to broker a ceasefire, but these demands that were laid upon them, on their side, they were unacceptable demands and they were unable to agree with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: So the negotiations continued, they went on for several hours, or for several days, or for how long? Because you were still there.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: That day, they went on for several hours. They then adjourned; Merdan went back to Zenica and Andric reported back to Mostar. They then reappeared the following day to conduct further negotiations, and that, again, happened during the morning. It was the morning where the body of Wayne Edwards was evacuated from Gornji Vakuf down to Split. Again, I presided -- at the same time that all this was going on, I was in the process of handing over my company, my command, to my successor, because I was being posted to Major Alun Jones, and so he had been there for the previous week, during all the build-up of tension and the fighting, and so that afternoon was when I actually handed over command of my company to Major Alun Jones and then departed up to Vitez, and then the following day leaving Vitez, back to Split, and then eventually out of theatre.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: On the basis of your observations during the negotiations, did you have the feeling that the local bosses really wanted a ceasefire, whereas persons who came from the outside -- that is, who represented Mostar -- took a much more rigid view and had many more demands in that regard?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: It was certainly -- and I was present at all the negotiations that took place, and it was always my impression that when the two local commanders were together, there was a determination to succeed in bringing about peace in Gornji Vakuf. And in fact, both showed quite a lot of personal courage, because on a number of occasions, at night -- they believed that the only way that they were going to stop the fighting was to go in person up to checkpoints, up to the front line, and actually instruct their soldiers not to fight. And so, along with some of my soldiers and they, themselves, approached checkpoints in the middle of the night and put themselves at risk to try and calm the situation down and try and implement some sort of ceasefire. Also, another thing that they tried to do was we also agreed to have negotiations with the lower commanders from the brigades, and so we arranged for -- what we believed to be the battalion commanders from the HVO side and the BiH side were all brought into the headquarters. We sent out armoured vehicles to pick them up, and they sat at each side of the table, fully armed, tired, excitable, but trying, trying to get some sort of ceasefire. And so that, as far as I was concerned, that showed, that reflected a determination at the local level to come to some sort of ceasefire. It was not successful, and my interpretation, my conclusion from that was that there was outside pressure that was preventing, you know, that from happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: For you, that outside pressure was from the Mostar people who were intervening at that point; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Certainly, during the negotiation, the more forthright and the more forceful demands were made by Andric, and there were threats made by him. And the reports that there were build-ups of brigades in Prozor of heavy equipment, we had sightings of tanks, we certainly saw tanks firing at the southern end of the town. This led us to believe that there was significant outside influence coming into the town of Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: As far as you know, these were outside HVO forces that were being used during the fighting in Gornji Vakuf; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, it was reported to me on numerous occasions that there was a build-up of forces in the Prozor area, and certainly some of the equipment that we saw had not been there in the past. It was new equipment which was being used, and we hadn't seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You have just said, Major Rule, that you were present in Gornji Vakuf during the days and weeks that preceded the conflict. I'm going to ask you to read two documents that I'm going to give you, the two last ones that I'm going to use this morning, and these both refer to the same facts. These are documents Z382,1 and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the interpreter did not get the last document number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What are these documents, Mr. Lopez-Terres?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) The two documents refer to a same press conference that was held on the 19th of January, 1993, in Busovaca, by the accused Dario Kordic, Colonel Blaskic, and Ignac Kostroman. The first, which has only one page, is an excerpt of that press conference as it was reproduced by the BBC. The second document comes from a magazine called Bojovnik, and this was an HVO magazine of that time in which there was a photograph of those who participated in the press conference, including Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The document which we have, one document we've been given, is numbered Z59,3. Something must have gone wrong with the translation. That appears to be the extract from Bojovnik. We've, I don't think, got the other item, which is numbered -- I forget.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) That's Z3821. Do you have them both, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We do. Let me just have a look at them. I think there may be some challenge. Do you object?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, we have not seen these, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, let's have a look at them first.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The actual objection is that both documents appear to refer to a press conference that was given on January the 19th, 1993, which is three days after Major Rule left his area of responsibility. So I don't -- in the absence of a foundation that he actually saw this press conference, we would object to it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me look at it. (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's right, Mr. Lopez-Terres, that the witness obviously was not present at the press conference or anything like that. But are you going to invite him to comment on the claims which are made about the number of armed soldiers and Mujahedin? Is that the purpose of what you want to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, that is, Your Honour. (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, clearly the witness can't give evidence about the press conference. He wasn't there; he doesn't know anything about it. But he can, it seems to us perfectly properly, make a comment about the claims which are being made about incidents in Gornji Vakuf which he does know about. So if you'd like to ask the witness if it was suggested that the BiH army sent to Gornji Vakuf about 2.000 armed soldiers as well as groups of Mujahedin, what would his comment be? You can put that. Well, Major Rule, you've heard the question. Perhaps you'd like to give us an answer.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: During the whole conflict, we maintained a presence in and around the area. We patrolled local villages, we patrolled the town. At no stage were significant reinforcements to the BiH ever reported to me whilst I was in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation).

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I have an additional question which is related to the press conference. During the time you were in Gornji Vakuf, did you see, were there any Muslim fighters that one ordinarily calls Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: I never saw that, no, and nor was it reported to me by my soldiers either.
