utterances.text: I know that it is hard for you to remember all the details, but approximately how much did you have to wait in order to be given this permission; five, seven, three hours, how long?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: No, no, no, not hours. Ten, fifteen minutes. The individuals were very wary about being engaged by the Croat position that was above them, and when he moved out to speak to us, he was taking cover. I was actually standing beside Colonel Stewart as he spoke to him, but he sort of ran out, dismissed us, ran back in again, and after a couple of more times, he eventually ran out, jumped into the driver's seat of the coach, drove the coach across, and I can't remember whether he actually moved -- I remember clearly mines with tilt switches on them. I think he may have moved one of those as well and then allowed -- which allowed us to go through and drive up to the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This fire which came in the direction of this Muslim position, from which position was it coming, what cardinal point, I mean; north, south? Could you show it on the map?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Well, we were sitting in the school which -- I'm trying to find exactly where the school is. It must have been about here, I suppose, about here (indicating). I can't make that out. It was about there, and we could see from over this area here (indicating) just off the map, on a piece of high ground, a knoll, a small hill, was sitting this gun which we could see, and we saw the trace of fire come down into the general vicinity down here. We couldn't actually see the roadblock itself from where we were, but we could certainly see that the Bofors gun and saw that the rounds were coming in in this direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So the fire was coming from the direction of north-northwest?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes. Very roughly, yes. If I had a proper map, I could probably be more accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear, sometime later, how long did this Muslim checkpoint exist in 1993? Since you left after a while, did you ever hear about how long it actually was in existence altogether?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: The following day, the recce party left the area of Vitez, but we left two liaison officers -- well, a small detachment of up to about five men, including two liaison officers and signallers, in the school. I probably came back up there four or five days later, and it was certainly gone by then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to see whether the BH army units remained at this location of this Bosna Construction Company premises, the plant, whether they were fortified there, around that area? Did you receive any reports in that regard or did you make your own observations?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: I wasn't based in Vitez, and you would probably be better asking somebody who was permanently based in Vitez about that. But certainly during the period immediately before the main regimental body came, I went up to Vitez on a couple of occasions and I didn't notice any significant military presence in that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now tell me, please, this same day when you first arrived there, when you found that barricade near Bila, that is, Mosunj, did you have any information that there was also a barricade erected by the Muslim forces due east, near the village of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: No, no, and the recce party wouldn't have been aware of that at all. It was certainly beyond the scope of the task that the recce party was attempting to conduct, so we wouldn't have been aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you learn, within the framework of your overall security considerations, whether there ever was a barricade erected in that area at that time?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Again, I wouldn't have been aware of that, because my zone of operations was to the south, and it wouldn't have been something with which I was concerned with, certainly not in that detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you ever, later on during your stay in Central Bosnia, see any Mujahedin units or any other units which also had Mujahedin elements in them?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: That was the only time that I remember seeing Mujahedin, in the pure sense of the word, i.e., wearing the Mujahedin clothing, the hat or whatever they call it, and being of sort of that ethnic grouping.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I can only take a step back to the markings of the barricade at Bila, could you, on the map -- perhaps I can ask the usher's assistance to give you a marker so that you can mark it for us. Could you please give the witness a marker so he can mark the location of the barricade which we just talked about so that we can have it in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: I remember that it was adjacent to some sort of cafe, because there was a television journalist who was attempting to drive through there and had been shot at and was taking cover in the cafe, and he assumed the cover of our convoy to drive out with us. His name was Dan Damon of Sky News. But I would say that that must be -- that the mark here looks pretty right to me, about there (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This would be, more or less, the exact location where this Muslim barricade was?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: I would rather look at a proper map in colour, but that is as accurate, I believe, as I can make it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Of course. Since you mentioned Mr. Dan Damon who filmed in that area, did he take any footage of the Mujahedin at that time, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: I don't believe he did. I think he was too concerned with getting out of that tight situation he was in. I think he was with his wife as well, but I don't believe they were filming at that stage, but I don't know. I can't remember having seen any news reports or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we can remove the small map and go back to 2612, the large colour map. Major, you're a professional soldier, so I am just going to assume that you read maps better than I do. But looking at the roads through the Lasva River Valley near Vitez, there are markings, two different numbers. This is in green. Do you know what these markings are? In the green box, there is an "E." Does that stand for "Europe" or "European route"?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yeah, I assumes it just stands for -- whether it stands for "Europe," I don't know, but it is a numerical and alphabetical designation for a specific road, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: May I conclude from it, and by also the way the road was marked, that this was a major road, that this was a thoroughfare?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes, very much so. This was a major road which could take large vehicles passing each other, tarmacked. Yes, a principal route.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct to assume that when you look at all of it, that it controls the main passage through Central Bosnia and that it connects through Bugojno and Jajce, connects to the major north-south routes?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do I conclude that and can you, as a soldier, say that this was a strategically-major road, that those who controlled this road controlled the entire area, the territory that the road covered?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: I'm slightly outside my area of expertise here, because this is an area which I didn't operate in on a daily basis. But certainly it is a significant route, control of which would be important.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you recall, either from personal observation or from reading about it, that there is major high ground surrounding this road, in other words, that there are mountains and hills?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: It's a wide valley. It's not a highly-precipitous valley. It is not like the valley that you see, sorry, coming up this road, for example (indicating), which is very, very steep on either side. It's almost, you know, sheer faces on either side. Here the valley is much wider (indicating). There are small hills, but the principal ranges are set further back from the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to another area. You said something about uniforms, but I think that you gave a response to my colleague, counsel for Mr. Kordic, so I will skip that. Now, I would like the usher to please show the witness 2983. Let me point you to the last paragraph above the sketch. From your previous responses in cross-examination, I concluded that there were all kinds of uniforms, that people were wearing whatever they could find. Could I conclude that the same sort applied to the vehicles as well?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it true that neither of the two sides in the Muslim-Croat conflict, or perhaps we can even include the Serbian forces, as a rule could not be recognised necessarily by the uniforms, by the weapons, and by vehicles? I'm talking about uniforms as part of the standard equipment or apparel.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that with regard to the Serbs. However, with regard to the HVO and BiH, there was generally a different uniform. The HVO had a sort of American-style, disruptive-pattern material generally, -- this is very general and it is a general rule -- whereas the BiH, their style of disruptive pattern was different and, I think, probably more reflected of what had been produced locally and perhaps what the Yugoslav national army may have worn. But I mean if you showed me the two varieties of combats, I could tell the difference. But it wasn't a hard and fast rule. It was only a general rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for the insignia on those uniforms worn by either army, were they always visible, were they always very clear? Or let me rephrase it. Your liaison officers, could they really draw reliable conclusions on the basis of the insignia which they saw?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I mean there were people that did not wear insignia. If soldiers were spotted without insignia, then no comment would have been made about it. I would say the majority, however, of soldiers did wear some form of insignia and which, you know, on reasonably close examination, you could tell one from the other. Again, not an absolute hard and fast rule but a general rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it then fair to conclude from all this that one needed to be more cautious when identifying and defining various groups, various troops, that is, whether one needs to pay more attention in order to determine which army some soldiers belonged to, to take a closer scrutiny of the insignia or uniforms or whatever; would that be true?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We didn't mention explicitly, neither you nor me, that we are talking about the Austrian markings on the -- Austrian flags and army signs on the vehicles; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: These were two vehicles which obviously had been -- I don't know how they were got hold of, but they obviously had recently been used by the Austrian army and they had somehow fallen into -- I remember this incident or this occurrence quite clearly, and they obviously hadn't even changed the tactical markings on them by that stage. I think they even still had Austrian number plates on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: To clarify it, the Austrian army was not part of the UNPROFOR in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: No, absolutely -- well, I don't believe they were. They certainly weren't operating in my area, and those vehicles were being used by HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So I can conclude that the Austrian armed forces were not involved in any manner as a sort of assistance to the HVO or something?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: No, I certainly don't believe so, and obviously secondhand military equipment, you know, can be got hold of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So I can conclude that these vehicles were bought at some army dumps or something; could one say that?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: I don't know where they came from, but it is a safe -- well, it could be assumed that they were purchased from some discarded military depot, you know, that the vehicles had passed their use within the Austrian army and had been sold on, which does happen, I know, certainly in the British army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: As if probably the case with those uniforms that you spoke about when my learned friend, Steve Sayers, asked you about them?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That is also part of what we already talked about, and that is that insignia were not really a reliable indication, various badges and insignia. They could not really be taken as a reliable sign, could they?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't agree with that statement. I would say that where badges were shown, they were a clear indication that they represented who they were required to represent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I see. But, for instance, the German flag on a soldier's uniform wasn't really a good basis for a conclusion that it was a German soldier, a member of the German army, was it?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes. The German surplus army uniform always carries a German flag on it, and it is worn all over Europe. What people don't wear, of course, is a BiH flash or an HVO flash, and where they were worn, then that was a clear indication to us that they represented the troops -- the badge represented the troops who wore them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Major Rule, may I read out to you just one sentence from your statement? I don't think we need to waste time in giving them to all. In your statement to the Tribunal investigators on the 27th and 28th of May, 1999, page 8, the first whole paragraph, you say that on the 13th of January, 1993, around 10.00 a.m., the meeting took place of the senior commanders, and that Colonel Andrijevic and Zeljko Siljek represented the HVO. You also said that Andrijevic was an HV officer from Tomislavgrad, whereas Siljek had come from Mostar, and that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was represented by General Merdan. You also told us today in your testimony. Then I also have a statement, also given to investigators on the 22nd of May, 1995, by Mr. Andrew David Williams, and he was your subordinate, and he said that he was your superior and that you were succeeded by Alun Jones. On page 3 of his statement, he said, "For the military in the northwest region of Herzegovina." If I may, just one more thing. Today you said explicitly that Merdan and Seljo represented the army of B and H and then Andrijevic and Siljek the HVO, and I should also like to show you 59/3, if it could be shown to the witness, Z59/3. Could you also get Z2985, please, Z298,5. If I may draw your attention to the last sentence in this second fragment. Please, before we begin, usher, will you please take also this document, 298,5, so as to have it at hand. Page 3, but will you just keep it at hand? We shall first finish with the first one. (In English) ... when we finish this, or maybe we can continue with the next one. (Interpretation) Major Rule, the document that you have before you --

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Is that correct, this one here?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It is, yes. The last sentence of this second paragraph, could you please read it?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: "Although Gornji Vakuf is not in the zone of responsibility of the Central Bosnia regional staff, Colonel Blaskic gave some information about the conflicts in this town."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now will you look at the second document, Z298,5, page 3? These two lines first.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Sorry, which two lines? The first two lines? "Colonel Andreivitch, the HVO Ops Zone commander, read the following message from his commander, a general in Mostar."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And on the basis of what we just saw and those two lines that you've just read out, would it be fair to conclude that Gornji Vakuf is not an Operative Zone in Central Bosnia, like Vitez and the whole area northeast of Gornji Vakuf? I hope I've jogged your memory with those two documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Unless the witness knows the answer to that, which I suspect he won't, it isn't really a matter for him. We shall have to hear evidence about it. Major Rule, do you know the answer to that question, or not?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: No, all I know is that the two commanders representing the HVO were -- I believed was a Colonel Andric, not Andrijevic, and I think there may have been a miswriting of it, and a Colonel Siljeg, who, I believed, came from Mostar. That is my memory of that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In other words, these papers did not remind you of anything more than what you already said when you were examined in relation to the accused Kordic, did they?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: They haven't changed my mind, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Fine. Good enough. Tell us, wasn't it natural -- rather, wasn't it necessary -- I correct myself -- for an officer of your rank to be acquainted, to be familiar with operative zones, at least in your area: Which was the chain of command, what was the hierarchy, who accounted to whom? Wouldn't it have made your job easier?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: I was, in the first instance, concerned very clearly with my immediate area of operations, and I've said before that I do believe, and even the HVO may -- I can't answer for them, but there was -- this was at a juncture where a number of areas of responsibility met; and whilst it may have sat in one particular zone, then it was influenced by a number of other zones as well. So I believe that other senior officers from other zones would have been very interested in what was happening at that location, and that shows -- or it would describe why this area was confusing in terms of the chain of command, and it was confusing to us as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And tell us, in the course of the negotiations between the Muslim and the Croat side -- and you told us about them; you told us that you tried to mediate and help -- did any of the HVO commanders mention that perhaps Blaskic should come, as the senior officer, or that they needed an authorisation from Blaskic as senior officer, or that Blaskic was his or their superior, or did Blaskic ever appear at such negotiations in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: I don't remember the name "Blaskic" being mentioned. And it was my feeling that the people representing the HVO were reporting directly back to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Then tell me, please, Major Rule, if, in your area of responsibility, in Gornji Vakuf, did you ever meet the accused Mario Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Mario Cerkez is a name that doesn't mean much -- it's not a name I know, and I don't remember having met anybody of that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In Central Bosnia as such, or in Gornji Vakuf alone?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: I don't know that name at all. If you showed me a photograph, I might recognise him; on the other hand, I might not. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (In English) This gentleman in the courtroom who is sitting on the right side to the security officer: Have you ever seen him?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: I can't be sure. The face does ring a vague bell, but I can't remember when. It does seem slightly familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (In English) Perhaps from the newspaper?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (In English) Thank you. Thank you. (Interpretation) Does "Djemal Merdan" mean anything to you? Does it remind you of anything?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes, I met him, and I would recognise him if I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it true that he was the commander of the 3rd Corps of the ABiH, or the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: I believe he was the deputy at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the 3rd Corps operated in the territory of Central Bosnia, including Gornji Vakuf and Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes. That was my understanding, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In other words, they operated over a very large territory?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes. And a corps is a large military organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell us, you already told us about that horrendous incident in November 1992, and if I understood you properly, you told us that this soldier came back from the front at Radusa. What kind of a front was that? Was it the front which the Muslims and Croats kept against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So at that time, in late 1992 and early 1993, you were aware that the Muslims and Croats jointly had a joint defence against Serbs at several places at different locations?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: I don't believe that the defence was joint. It was certainly a defence line, but the two areas were separate, and certainly, during that time, there wasn't significant fighting in that region.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So they had different sectors along the front line against the Serbs, against the Chetniks, JNA; that is what I mean.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: I went to visit, to observe the front line once, and it was clear that the two -- certainly that where I saw, there were two separate areas. They didn't operate together; they operated separately. They had two different sectors, or perhaps a number of different sectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: As a civilian, were those sectors -- did all those sectors serve as a defence against the Serbs, regardless of whether they were separated or not?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: I'm a little bit unclear exactly as to what actually took place up at that front line. I knew that there had been fighting, but certainly whilst I was in Gornji Vakuf, there wasn't a great deal of fighting at that time. But ostensibly, I was aware that there was a joint front line held by both HVO and BiH, as there was in Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard that they held a joint defence line separated into sectors, that is true, on Vlasic, west of Travnik, at Turbe?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Again, outside of my area of intimate knowledge, but I believe that there was some sort of joint defence up there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, it's now 5 to 4.00. The witness has been cross-examined for about the same time as he was examined in chief, and I really think it's probably time to call it a day. Is there very much more you want to ask him about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I don't think really too much, only a couple of questions, and more or less only of clarifying nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Major Rule, very briefly, please, will you try to be as succinct as possible. Did you personally visit local commanders, either of the HVO or the ABiH? Did you ever visit them on their premises? Were there any such instances? "Yes" or "No," please.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes, frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And on those occasions, your safety was presumably one of the factors, I mean, your personal safety? Was it a matter of concern?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes, I had to be aware of placing myself in a dangerous position, yes. Sometimes --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But tell me, if you used a vehicle to go there, would it be an APC or some other type of armoured vehicle?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Where in particular? Are you talking about the headquarters, or going to a front line?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to headquarters.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes. I would generally go in a Land Rover, if I knew that there wasn't any report of fighting in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And would you have armed escort? I don't know, one, two, soldiers, with you, escorting you?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes, I would always take an escort with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And the escort would be with you right to the door of the office in which you had those meetings?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes, but the escort wouldn't be involved in the meetings. I would -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, naturally.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: They would be outside the door, but sometimes I would take my company sergeant-major or my company liaison officer with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it true it is from some other meetings, from meetings with (indiscernible), and as to the escort, these guards, these soldiers usually had rifles, not only pistols and small arms?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: They would be carrying rifles, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (In English) Sir, may I conclude that security was really actually highly visible?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: There were two British soldiers, wearing uniforms that were clearly British, and carrying long-barrelled weapons, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (In English) Certainly the policy was not low profile?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (In English) Thank you. Okay. Let's go further.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: If I drove to Bugojno when I knew it was shelling, I would make sure that I was in an armoured vehicle. If I was going near a front line, I perhaps wouldn't be quite so visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mentioned this unit, the unit belonging to the Tiger Brigade, and my learned friend on Kordic's defence team asked you about this. But just one question: After that, have you ever again received an information, a report, about spotting any unit with HV insignia north of Mostar? "Yes" or "No" only, please.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At some point, you told us -- and let's not go back and waste any time; it is Exhibit 2481, and it was a request for the authorisation of 250 shells of 120 millimetres from the SPS factory; you remember what it's all about. You were asked about it, and you told us that it was quite possible to transport, those 150-or-so shells could be very easily transported. How many vehicles does one need for 150 120-millimetre shells? One, two, three, or how many?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: It depends how they are packaged, but if they are in their normal packaging, I would estimate that -- two, possibly three vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Trucks, you mean?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And let me ask you, which route would you take to do this? You said that they would be going from Vitez to Gornji Vakuf; which route would they take?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: I'm not aware of -- I was only shown that -- that message today, and I'm not sure what -- exactly where they were coming from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, but before, you hypothetically said it was possible, I mean trucks, that is, they could be transported. Did I understand you properly?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But I'm wondering -- I just wonder, again, hypothetically, was it possible in terms of road, in terms of an accessible route, of an open route, whether there was such a free passage for them?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: I just don't know. I don't know of the vehicles, I don't know where they would have come from, I don't know what routes they might have used. There were a number of very circuitous routes that could have been used.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you think that in early 1993, there were possible routes which the HVO could use to transport weapons to another HVO area without --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Kovacic, we've heard enough about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (In English) Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, have you got anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (In English) I'm just checking, Your Honour. I'm asking just for one minute to check. Your Honours, I believe I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I have a few clarifications, very rapidly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Major Rule, on several occasions, mention was made of the population of Gornji Vakuf. I looked at the numbers, the figures for that population, and the census of 1991 gives us some figures. Would you agree to say that the following figures, that the Croatian population of Gornji Vakuf was 42,5 per cent, the Muslim population was 55,8, and the Serb population was 0,4? Would you agree with those figures?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: The Serb population was 0,4? Certainly I agree with the Muslim and the Croatian figures. I certainly remember being told at Gornji Vakuf that the Muslim population was higher than that; it was more like 6 or 7 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The Serbian population?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: The Serbs, yes. But I may have been wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In respect of the incident of the 18th of November and the beheading of the handicapped person, I thought that I understood that during the negotiations which you conducted with the HVO and representatives of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that the incident was mentioned on several occasions, and even undermined, to some extent, the negotiations. During those negotiations, was any mention made of the return of the soldier to the front, and if so, did the HVO deny the fact that the soldier had gone back to the front?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Are you talking about the stage of the initial -- when it was reported to me, and then the initial negotiation? No, that wasn't reported to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Subsequently?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: It was subsequently. I can't remember the exact date. It was subsequently reported to me, I think, shortly before I left, that this individual had been seen on the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Were you able to question the officials of the HVO about that return, or that possible, alleged return of the soldier to the front lines?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: No, I never did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In respect of the bomb that was placed near the BH army headquarters in that hotel that it occupied on the night of the 11th of January, I believe it was, is it possible, in your opinion, that the bomb was put there by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Highly unlikely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Is it plausible, in your opinion, that the BH army would itself have put the bomb into its own institution?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Highly unlikely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: As regards the presence of those soldiers wearing the Tiger insignia on their left sleeves -- I think it was the left sleeves of their uniforms -- when you learned about that information, in the reports that were given, did it state that those were uniforms that were similar for all the soldiers? Were they new uniforms or surplus uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: I certainly recall at the time that it was more than simply a Tigers badge. The patrols reported that they appeared to be more professional-looking; they appeared to be smarter, neater, and equipped uniformly, as a regular soldier would look. And a regular soldier would be able to pinpoint another regular soldier. He would also be able to differentiate between an irregular soldier as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Do you remember whether at that time it might have been mentioned that it was excess gear, excess uniforms, surplus?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: No. I mean, I mentioned before that generally, as a general rule, the Croatians wore this U.S.-style -- I don't know whether it was manufactured there or manufactured locally, but this disrupted pattern was the same style as the United States disrupted-pattern material, and that is generally what Croatian soldiers, Croatian HVO, wore. The Muslims were far less uniform in what they wore, but they generally wore one thing or another. These people were wearing, I believe were wearing webbing equipment, were wearing a combat uniform that was matching.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Were you told at the time that beyond -- or beside the Tiger insignia, the soldiers also were carrying an Austrian, a German, or a British flag on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: No. No, I'd just like to say that, you know, if there was a German flag, then it was obviously -- you know, worn because the uniform that they were wearing was from German surplus requirements. If somebody was wearing a Croatian insignia or a Muslim or Bosnian, BiH insignia, it was very clear to us that they -- what side they were on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: As far as you know, is there a Tiger Regiment in the HVO military organisation?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: In the HVO military organisation? I don't believe so. We were aware of the Tiger formation in the HV army, and we were aware that it had a reputation, but I wasn't aware of any HVO unit that wore a Tigers badge, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Do you know where that Croatian army unit was stationed, the one that had the Tiger insignia?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: I can't be specific. I think -- possibly -- possibly Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Major Rule, on two or three occasions, I believe, the Defence asked you what your comments were about the civil war that was going on in the region. I also would have a question about that. Are you an expert in international criminal military law? Are you an expert in the question of international armed conflicts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going to have to deal with all these problems. The witness gives the evidence. There's no need to answer, Major Rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Your Honour. I have one further question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I believe that the witness had located the name that he was looking for in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you give it to us, please?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. My last question, about the Lasva Valley, referred to Colonel Stewart's book, "Broken Lives." You said, and I think I understood you, that you didn't always agree with Colonel Stewart?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: That's certainly -- you know, certainly nothing unusual in a unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: My last question would be the final one referring to this book, page 207, on the part that has to do with the Gornji Vakuf battle, which is, as I say on page 207, Colonel Stewart said: "It seemed that the Croats were trying to take the city from their positions in the hills." Would you agree, for once, with Colonel Stewart about that way of looking at the conflict in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, from the southern hills, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Major Rule, that concludes your evidence. You are released. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give your evidence. Half past 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 4.10 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 28th day of July, 1999, at 9.30 a.m. 24 25
